# 2. Technical details

Our goal was to classify kangaroo skulls as giganteus, melanops or fuliginosus using 18 skull measurements and sex. Most of these measurements might be strongly correlated, since they largely reflect overall skull size.

```{r}
# Plot 1: Predictors used (1): nasal.length
ggplot(kangaroos, aes(x = species, y = nasal.length, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Nasal Length Distributions Across Species",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Nasal Length (mm)",
    caption = "Figure 1"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") 
```

```{r}
# Plot 2: Predictors used (2): crest.width & mandible.depth
ggplot(kangaroos, aes(x = crest.width, y = mandible.depth, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, position = "jitter") +
  labs(
    title = "Crest Width by Mandible Depth",
    x = "Crest Width(mm)",
    y = "Mandible Depth(mm)",
    caption = "Figure 2"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Plot 3: Predictors used (2): zygomatic.width & sex
  ggplot(kangaroos, aes(x = zygomatic.width, fill = species)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_wrap("sex") +
  labs(
    title = "Species by Zygomatic Width Faceted by Sex",
    x = "Zygomatic Width(mm)",
    y = "Density",
    caption = "Figure 3"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

A single deep classification tree would therefore depend heavily on which of several nearly interchangeable measurements it happened to split on, which makes it unstable and prone to overfitting. We used a random forest instead. Averaging many decorrelated trees reduces that variance, and the forest still lets us rank which measurements matter most.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 8

# STEP 1: tree specification with specific tuning parameter values
tree_spec <- decision_tree() |>
  set_mode("classification") |> 
  set_engine(engine = "rpart") |> 
  set_args(cost_complexity = 0, min_n = 2, tree_depth = 30)

# STEP 2: Build the tree!
# Note that we specified our tuning parameters in Step 1.
# Thus no tuning (hence no workflows) necessary.
kangaroo_tree <- tree_spec |> 
  fit(species ~ ., data = kangaroos)

# Plot the tree
kangaroo_tree |> 
  extract_fit_engine() |> 
  plot(margin = 0) 
kangaroo_tree |> 
  extract_fit_engine() |> 
  text(cex = 0.7)
```

Species was treated as a categorical response, with all 19 other variables as predictors. Of the 148 skulls, 47 were missing at least one measurement and were dropped, leaving 101 complete cases. We grew 500 classification trees, each on a bootstrap sample of those 101 skulls. At each split, 4 of the 19 predictors were randomly chosen as candidates, and the split minimising Gini impurity was chosen. Trees were grown deep, with a minimum node size of 2, and each skull's class is the majority vote across trees. These were default settings and were not tuned. We set the random seed to 253.

```{r}
# There's randomness behind the splits!

set.seed(253)
    
# STEP 1: Model Specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest()  |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  set_engine(engine = "ranger") |> 
  set_args(
    mtry = NULL,
    trees = 500,
    min_n = 2,
    probability = FALSE,    # Report classifications, not probability calculations
    importance = "impurity" # Use Gini index to measure variable importance
  )
    
# STEP 2: Build the forest
# There are no preprocessing steps or tuning, hence no need for a workflow!
kangaroo_forest <- rf_spec |> 
  fit(species ~ ., data = kangaroos)

kangaroo_forest
```

We estimated performance with out-of-bag (OOB) error: each skull is classified using only the one-third of trees whose bootstrap samples left it out. The OOB error was 24.75%, so we expect about 75.25% of new skulls to be classified correctly. Guessing the most common species would get about 34% right as per the no information rate (NIR) calculated from the confusion matrix below.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# The cbind() includes the original candy data
# alongside their predicted popularity levels
kangaroo_forest |> 
  predict(new_data = kangaroos) |> 
  cbind(kangaroos) |> 
  conf_mat(
    truth = species,
    estimate = .pred_class
  )
```

```{r}
#Overall accuracy
(49+42+35)/148
```

The confusion matrix shows a clear pattern in the errors. Fuliginosus is almost always identified correctly (49 of 50). Nearly all misclassifications are between giganteus and melanops: 11 melanops skulls were labelled giganteus, and 7 giganteus skulls were labelled melanops. Even when predicting its own training data, the forest cannot fully separate these two species, which points to real overlap in their skull measurements.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 10
# Print the metrics
kangaroo_forest |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  pluck("variable.importance") |> 
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)
    
# Plot the metrics
library(vip)
kangaroo_forest |> 
  vip(geom = "point", num_features = 20)
```

Variable importance, measured by the total decrease in Gini impurity, ranks nasal length, crest width, and zygomatic width highest, followed by mandible width and nasal width. Sex contributes almost nothing. Figures 1–3 show how these top predictors are distributed across species.\
